For energy estimates for hyperbolic differential equations, one generally uses the differential form of Gronwall’s inequality, a form which is also mentioned in the TODO section of Mathlib/Analysis/ODE/Gronwall.lean.

I have therefore decided to formalise the following theorem.

As I have only recently started working with Lean, I am concerned that
my formalisation may be rather cumbersome. I have tried to keep the
code as clear as possible and have avoided using private macros. I
was, however, tempted to introduce more parentheses. For example, I
would have preferred to write u (y) / v (y) rather than u y / v y.

Do I need to open a pull request (fork, clone, new branch, code, add, commit, push)? Open a RP

As for documentation, I have recently been using literate programming.
Once the code is complete, a meta-file is produced (as an Emacs user,
I use Org mode, in which the documentation is written in LaTeX around
the code, so that both the code and the LaTeX file can be extracted).

Since very few users are likely to use Emacs, I could provide the
LaTeX file alongside the Lean file, and, to be on the safe side,
include the PDF as well.

Uwe Brauer

GronwallVariableCoeff.lean?

I'm not sure if I'm understanding you correctly;
If you mean that you think the material belongs in a separate file, then that's perfectly fine, as long as there's a reason for not putting it in the existing file (e.g. it requires a smaller/larger set of imports, it doesn't fit the purpose of the file, etc).
If you actually mean just for the purpose of review then not really, because the goal is to review the finished product, including location.

There are two reasons why I am hesitant to copy my code directly into Gronwall.lean.

  1. Authorship: Gronwall.lean was implemented by Yury Kudryashov in 2020. I would therefore need to add a line with my name and the year.

  2. Testing: I am not sure whether I would be able to test everything properly after adding my code. I would use VS Code and, of course, something along the lines of lake env lean Gronwall.lean.

By the way, although I think it would be better to raise this as a separate question, surely there is a distinction between LLM-generated and LLM-assisted code?

1. If you've added/changed a significant amount of the file (say 20%) you could add your name to the Authors: list. The year says when the file was created, not modified. The detailed history is saved on GitHub; the header represents who's responsible for maintaining the code, not authorship per se.
  2. You don't need to lake ... if you're using VS Code, and also Mathlib has CI that runs automatically and tests everything works. If you open a PR you'll see at the bottom stuff that's loading, and when it finishes it'll show either :cross_mark: or :check:

  3. Can you define the distinction? But also it's not super important, as the AI guidelines say:

    If you use artificial intelligence, you must explain this in the PR description. Explain which tool(s) you used and how you used it. This provides useful context for reviewers: tools make different mistakes than humans, so knowing this makes it easier to spot common errors.

    You can explain any nuances in the PR description. You can also use this format if you'd like; some contributors use it but there's no mandated format.
